rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call has no crookedness: the caller neither turns aside from the addressee nor away from him.
rows.anchor: دعوتني دعوة لا عوج لك عنها أي إني لا أعوج لك ولا عنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humsa is glossed either as the sound of feet moving to the gathering place or as a faint, quiet sound.
rows.anchor: يقال: نقل الأقدام إلى المحشر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas cites a poetic line whose humaysā describes the soft sound of camels’ hoof coverings as they walk.
rows.anchor:
وذكر عن 114 ب ابن عباس أنه تمثل:
وهن يمشين بنا هميسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the exception, man is accusative as the object of benefit: intercession benefits only the person God permits someone to intercede for.
rows.anchor: لا تنفع إلا من أذن له أن يشفع فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being pleased with someone’s statement parallels being pleased with his deed; Arabic can also say one is pleased with a deed for someone or from him.
rows.anchor: كقولك : ورضي منه عمله وقد يقول الرجل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ones who do not know what lies before or behind them are the angels whom people worship; only God knows it, as they cannot encompass Him in knowledge.
rows.anchor: يعني ملائكته الذين عبدهم من عبدهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faces’ humbling means submission and obedience, as in saying that one has submitted and obeyed another.
rows.anchor: عنوت لك: خضعت لك وأطعتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An explanation pictures a Muslim placing his hands, forehead, and knees on the ground while bowing and prostrating.
rows.anchor: وذكر أيضا أنه وضع المسلم يديه وجبهته وركبتيه إذا سجد وركع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression that land did not ʿanat means it produced nothing; the two forms are equivalent, like the paired forms for casting dust.
rows.anchor: ويقال الأرض لم تعن بشيء أي لم تنبت شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking something ʿanwatan can mean seizure by force or taking it with the other party’s submission and obedience.
rows.anchor: والعنوة في قول العرب: أخذت هذا الشيء عنوة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses ʿanwatan for a taking secured through submission, not fighting.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر .
فما أخذوها عنوة عن مودة ... ولكن بضرب المشرفي استقالها
فهذا على معنى الطاعة والتسليم بلا قتال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadm is reducing or deducting something from a person’s rightful due.
rows.anchor: هضمت لك من حقي أي حططته

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: When asked after the Battle of the Camel whether the matter was a deduction or retribution, Ali said what lay beneath his feet was forfeited; Farrāʾ glosses that as loss.
rows.anchor: وجاء عن علي بن أبي طالب في يوم الجمل أنه قيل له أهضم أم قصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikran can mean honor, as in God’s description of the Qur’an as a reminder and honor for the addressee and his people.
rows.anchor: شرفا وهو مثل قول الله (وإنه لذكر لك ولقومك)

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: A second gloss takes dhikran as punishment: they remember the arrival of the punishment they had been promised.
rows.anchor: ويقال (أو يحدث لهم ذكرا) عذابا أي يتذكرون حلول العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet hurried to recite revelation before Gabriel had finished; he was told to wait until Gabriel completed it.
rows.anchor: كان صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا أتاه جبريل بالوحي عجل بقراءته قبل أن يستتم جبريل تلاوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here forgetting means leaving what one had been commanded to do.
rows.anchor: وقوله (فنسي) ترك ما أمر به.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qāniʿ is a person who asks and accepts whatever is given; the muʿtarr silently approaches the slaughter but does not ask.
rows.anchor: القانع: الذي يسألك (فما أعطيته من شيء ) قبله. والمعتر: ساكت يتعرض لك عند الذبيحة، ولا يسألك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readers agree on the masculine form yanālu; the feminine tanālu would also be correct.
rows.anchor: ولو قيل (تنال) كان صوابا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pagans used to splash sacrificial blood around the Kaaba, and Muslims wanted to do likewise; the verse redirects the offering toward God-fearing sincerity rather than flesh or blood.
rows.anchor: فلما حج المسلمون أرادوا مثل ذلك فأنزل الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: أكثر القراء
rows.claim: Most readers recite yudāfiʿ, which Farrāʾ himself reads; yudfaʿ is also mentioned as a variant.
rows.anchor: وأكثر القراء على (يدافع) وبه أقرأ.

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي
rows.claim: Al-Sulamī is reported to read yudāfiʿ and the corresponding verbal noun difāʿ; Farrāʾ accepts both as correct.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي (يدافع)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the reading yuqātilūn, the sense is that God permitted those who are fighting to fight.
rows.anchor: أذن الله للذين يقاتلون أن يقاتلوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading says they are fought because they were wronged; it conveys the same permission to fight, and Farrāʾ accepts both.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أذن لهم أن يقاتلوا وكل صواب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expelled believers had done nothing except say that God is their Lord.
rows.anchor: يقول لم يخرجوا إلا بقولهم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing puts the exceptive phrase in the genitive, governed by the preposition in bi-ghayri haqq.
rows.anchor: في موضع خفض ترده على الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase is an exception, as in the construction except seeking the face of his Lord.
rows.anchor: جعلت (أن) مستثناة كما قال (إلا ابتغاء وجه ربه الأعلى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He identifies ṣawāmiʿ as Christian monks’ hermitages, biyaʿ as Christian prayer places, ṣalawāt as Jewish synagogues, and masājid as Muslim mosques.
rows.anchor: الصوامع للرهبان وأما الصلوات فهي كنائس اليهود والمساجد (مساجد الإسلام)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding clause means God protects each prophet’s religion through followers until He sent Muhammad.
rows.anchor: يدفع بأمره وأتباعه عن دين كل نبي إلى أن بعث الله محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers treating the well and palace as genitives coordinated with roofs, accepting the syntactic sequence even though the spatial meaning of ʿalā fits roofs better.
rows.anchor: البئر والقصر يخفضان على العطف على العروش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, if the well and palace are outside the village, they can be governed by min, meaning many a village, and many a well and palace.
rows.anchor: إذا نويت أنهما ليسا من القرية- بمن كأنك قلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-khabʾ is the hidden or unseen thing in the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: وهو الغيب غيب السموات وغيب الأرض

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: Another gloss identifies the hidden thing as rainwater from heaven and plants from earth.
rows.anchor: هو الماء الذي ينزل من السماء والنبت من الأرض

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah’s reading has min, from, where the common wording has fī, in; Farrāʾ says either preposition can be dropped in the idiom without changing the sense.
rows.anchor: في قراءة عبد الله (يخرج الخبء من السموات)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction to turn away and then see the reply is a semantic ordering: Solomon urges the hoopoe to hurry, then look at the response.
rows.anchor: ثم أخر (فانظر ماذا يرجعون) ومعناها التقديم.

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: Another account says the hoopoe left the letter, hid from the queen, and watched from a window in her chamber.
rows.anchor: ففعل: ألقى الكتاب وطار إلى كوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The letter is called noble because it was sealed, according to what Farrāʾ was told.
rows.anchor: جعلته كريما لأنه كان مختوما

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: Another account says the queen called it noble because she had seen a king’s letter and associated nobility with its author.
rows.anchor: وصفت الكتاب بالكرم لقومها لأنها رأت كتاب ملك عندها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the suggestion that she called it noble before learning it was from Solomon, since she had read it before leaving for her council.
rows.anchor: قبل أن تعلم أنه من سليمان. وما يعجبني ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both instances of inna are read with kasra; opening them with fatḥa is also grammatical, with their positions analyzed as apposition or as accusatives after an omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: ولو فتحتا جميعا كان جائزا

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading has wa-an before the basmala, which supports opening the particle; an opened an joined to a clause is lightened.
rows.anchor: في قراءة أبي (وأن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial alif of alā is always open; the phrase can be nominative as a repetition of the preceding report or accusative if the preposition is omitted.
rows.anchor: فألفها مفتوحة لا يجوز كسرها. وهي في موضع رفع إذا كررتها على (ألقي) ونصب على:

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah’s reading repeats inna in both clauses, which Farrāʾ takes as evidence for kasra because the clauses connect to the preceding inna.
rows.anchor: في قراءة عبد الله (وإنه من سليمان وإنه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw is omitted before the recitation clause to make it an imperative; Arabic amara permits either an أن-clause or a direct command, as shown by the cited examples.
rows.anchor: قد أسقطت منها الواو للجزم على جهة الأمر

rows.speaker: العقيلي
rows.claim: A line recited by al-ʿUqaylī treats the first occurrence of ʿām in the phrase year after year as redundant.
rows.anchor: العقيلي. فالعام الأول فضل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wakaza means struck or punched him.
rows.anchor: وقوله: (فوكزه موسى) يريد: فلكزه»

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads fa-nakazahu; wahazahu is another Arabic form, and all three verbs mean the same thing.
rows.anchor: قراءة عبد الله (فنكزه) ووهزه أيضا لغة. كل سواء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-qaḍā ʿalayhi means that Moses killed him.
rows.anchor: وقوله (فقضى عليه) يعني قتله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses regretted what happened, sought God’s forgiveness, and was forgiven.
rows.anchor: وندم موسى فاستغفر الله فغفر له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Moses did not qualify his promise, so he was tested; lan akūna is a statement about Moses.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لم يستثن فابتلي، فجعل (لن) خبرا لموسى.

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads fa-lā tajʿalnī, making the clause a prayer: Moses asks God not to make him an accomplice of wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة عبد الله (فلا تجعلني ظهيرا) فقد تكون (لن أكون) على هذا المعنى دعاء من موسى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelite later summoned Moses against another Egyptian; Moses rebuked him for having killed one man the day before, and the Israelite exposed Moses as the killer.
rows.anchor: أي قد قتلت بالأمس رجلا فتدعوني إلى آخر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses headed for the water of Midian; Midian is indeclinable because it is the name of a town.
rows.anchor: مدين لم تصرف لأنها اسم لتلك البلدة.

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses Madian without declension, illustrating the town name’s grammatical treatment.
rows.anchor:
وقال الشاعر
رهبان مدين لو رأوك تنزلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some codices have ḥusnan; Farrāʾ says it and iḥsānan have the same meaning.
rows.anchor: (حسنا) وكذلك هي في مصاحفهم، ومعناهما واحد والله أعلم.

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah’s reading adds istawā before reaching full maturity; Farrāʾ says the reordered wording has the same sense because Arabic can mention a later event before an earlier one.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة عبد الله: حتى إذا استوى وبلغ أشده وبلغ أربعين سنة

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: One view identifies ashudd here with age forty.
rows.anchor: إن الأشدها هنا هو الأربعون

rows.speaker: بعض المشيخة
rows.claim: An account from some elders assigns age thirty-three to ashudd and forty to istiwāʾ.
rows.anchor: وسمعت بعض المشيخة يذكر بإسناد له في الأشد: ثلاث وثلاثون، وفي الاستواء: أربعون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farrāʾ prefers thirty-three as ashudd followed by forty as istiwāʾ, since the numbers form a closer sequence; he says eighteen could also work if joined to forty.
rows.anchor: والأول أشبه بالصواب لأن الأربعين أقرب في النسق إلى ثلاث وثلاثين ومنها إلى ثماني عشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashudd is eighteen in another passage; the example of less than two-thirds, half, and a third illustrates that nearby quantities form a better sequence.
rows.anchor: وسمعت أن الأشد في غير هذا الموضع: ثمانى عشرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, through the continuation about those whose best deeds are accepted.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: نزلت في أبي بكر رحمه الله

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Waththāb and some of Abdullah’s companions read the acceptance and overlooking verbs with first-person nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يحيى بن وثاب، وذكرت عن بعض أصحاب عبد الله: «نتقبل عنهم أحسن ما عملوا ونتجاوز عن سيئاتهم» بالنون.

rows.speaker: قراءة العوام
rows.claim: The common reading uses third-person yāʾ in both verbs; a second-person feminine reading would also be correct.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العوام: «يتقبل عنهم أحسن ما عملوا ويتجاوز عن سيئاتهم» بالياء وضمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waʿd al-ṣidq is like waʿdan ṣidqan; a verbal noun meaning truly is accusative whether definite or indefinite, as in God’s promise truly.
rows.anchor: كقولك: وعدا صدقا، أضيف إلى نفسه، وما كان من مصدر في معنى حقا فهو نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikrāhum is nominative with an understood lahum: what reminder could they have when the Hour comes? The parallel says that later remembrance and regret will not help.
rows.anchor: بلهم، والمعنى: فإني لهم ذكراهم إذا جاءتهم الساعة؟

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah’s reading describes the revealed chapter as muḥdatha, a newly revealed sura.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة عبد الله: سورة محدثة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a fighting verse was revealed, Muslims feared the burden and possible abrogation; they wished for another sura, then disliked the command once fighting was prescribed.
rows.anchor: وذكره شق عليهم وتواقعوا أن تنسخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samʿun wa-ṭāʿatun is the ordinary nominative Arabic response to a command, whether the command feels burdensome or not.
rows.anchor: فالطاعة مرفوعة في كلام العرب إذا قيل لهم: افعلوا كذا وكذا، فثقل عليهم أو لم يثقل قالوا: سمع وطاعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farrāʾ reads fa-awlā as a threat to those who disliked the sura, then restarts with lahum ṭāʿatun wa-qawlun maʿrūf; he calls this the Arabic reading.
rows.anchor:
فصارت:
فأولى وعيدا لمن كرهها، واستأنف الطاعة بلهم، والأول عندنا كلام العرب، وقول الكلبي هذا غير مردود.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas’s transmitted parsing likewise makes fa-awlā a threat, then starts a new statement addressed to the believers among them about obedience and good speech; Farrāʾ does not reject it.
rows.anchor:
عن ابن عباس قال:
قال الله عز وجل: (فأولى) ثم قال لهم للذين آمنوا منهم طاعة وقول معروف، فصارت:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has fatḥa on the sīn in ʿasaytum; Nāfiʿ of Medina reads the sīn with kasra, a rare dialectal form.
rows.anchor: قرأها العوام بنصب السين ، وقرأها نافع المدني: فهل عسيتم، بكسر السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra may reflect Arabic alteration of a defective verb that lacks a full conjugation, as speakers also vary forms of laysa; ʿasā likewise has no yafʿalu form.
rows.anchor: ولعلها لغة نادرة، وربما اجترأت العرب على تغيير بعض اللغة إذا كان الفعل لا يناله قد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawallaytum can mean taking charge of people’s affairs, after which they corrupt the land and sever kinship.
rows.anchor: إن توليتم أمور الناس أن تفسدوا في الأرض، وتقطعوا أرحامكم

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: Alternatively, if they turn away from Muhammad, they may return to their former disbelief, corruption, and severing of kinship.
rows.anchor: ويقال: ولعلكم إن انصرفتم عن محمد صلى الله عليه، وتوليتم عنه أن تصيروا إلى أمركم الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawwala means that Satan adorned their deeds, while God granted them respite.
rows.anchor: زين لهم وأملي لهم الله

rows.speaker: الأعمش وعاصم
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim share the active reading; reports also attribute it to Ali, Ibn Masʿud, and Zayd ibn Thābit.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قرأها الأعمش وعاصم، وذكر عن علي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads amlā with an unhamzated yāʾ, making God the speaker of the verb.
rows.anchor: وذكر عن مجاهد أنه قرأها: (وأملى لهم) مرسلة الياء، يخبر الله جل وعز عن نفسه

rows.speaker: بعض أهل المدينة
rows.claim: Some Medinans use a passive form, with ḍamma on the alif and fatḥa on the yāʾ; the meaning is close.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض أهل المدينة: وأملى لهم بنصب الياء وضم الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening refers to Hudaybiyya, where there was only a little fighting by stone throwing; fatḥ can mean a peace settlement or taking something by force.
rows.anchor: كان فتح وفيه قتال [قليل] مراماة بالحجارة، فالفتح قد يكون صلحا، ويكون أخذ الشيء عنوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāʾirat al-sūʾ means punishment, like rajul al-sūʾ; sūʾ is the more common form, while Arabs rarely say dāʾirat al-sūʾ.
rows.anchor: مثل قولك: رجل السوء، ودائرة السوء: العذاب، والسوء أفشى في اللغة وأكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Litūminū means that whoever believes believes in the Prophet; the addressed form can refer to a group even if only some members act.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: ليؤمن بك من آمن، ولو قيل: ليؤمنوا لأن المؤمن غير المخاطب

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Taʿazzirūhu means support the Prophet with the sword, as reported from al-Kalbī.
rows.anchor: تنصروه بالسيف كذلك ذكره عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s hand over their hands refers to fidelity to the pledge and covenant.
rows.anchor: يد الله فوق أيديهم (10) بالوفاء والعهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who stayed behind at Hudaybiyya were desert Arabs from Aslam, Juhayna, Muzayna, and Ghifār; they claimed family and property kept them back and thought the Messenger would not return.
rows.anchor: الذين تخلفوا عن الحديبية: شغلتنا أموالنا وأهلونا، وهم أعراب: أسلم، وجهينة، ومزينة، وغفار

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Waththāb alone uses ḍamma on ḍād in ḍurr; ʿĀṣim, Medinans, and al-Ḥasan use fatḥa, all vocalizing the word for harm differently.
rows.anchor: ضم يحيى بن وثاب وحده الضاد، ونصبها عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s sight did not turn left or right, overstep, or exceed what he saw.
rows.anchor: بصر محمد صلى الله عليه ما زاغ بقلبه يمينا وشمالا ولا طغى ولا جاوز ما رأى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common form is light in the tāʾ; al-Kisāʾī pauses with hāʾ, while Farrāʾ himself pauses with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء. وأنا أقف على التاء.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says a man used to prepare sawiq for people at al-Lāt and reads the tāʾ doubled, associating the name with that activity.
rows.anchor:
عن مجاهد قال:
كان رجلا يلت لهم السويق، وقرأها: اللات والعزى فشدد التاء.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a merchant prepared and sold sawiq near the idol al-Lāt, which was named after him and worshipped by Thaqīf; al-ʿUzzā was an acacia worshipped by Ghatafān.
rows.anchor:
ابن عباس قال:
كان رجل من التجار يلت السويق لهم عند اللات وهو- الصنم وببيعه فسميت بذلك الرجل، وكان صنما- لثقيف، وكانت العزى سمرة- لغطفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāt was a rock worshipped by Hudhayl and Khuzāʿa.
rows.anchor: كانت مناة صخرة لهذيل، وخزاعة يعبدونها.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to destroy al-ʿUzzā; Khālid did so while reciting a taunt that the idol had been humiliated by God.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه خالد بن الوليد إلى العزى ليقطعها قال: ففعل وهو يقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pagans called idols and angels God’s daughters; the verse rebukes them for reserving sons for themselves and assigning daughters to God, an unjust division.
rows.anchor: لأنهم قالوا: هذه الأصنام والملائكة بنات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers do not hamza ḍīzā; some Arabs use hamza, but no known reader does. Farrāʾ analyzes it as fiʿlā and explains the initial kasra by the pattern’s relation to the forms of the dual, plural, and feminine singular.
rows.anchor: والقراء جميعا لم يهمزوا- ضيزي، ومن العرب من يقول: قسمة ضيزى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr madīnīn means not owned or enslaved; he has also heard the gloss rewarded.
rows.anchor: غير مدينين (86) مملوكين، وسمعت: مجزيين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who are among the close ones belong to the Garden of Eden.
rows.anchor: من المقربين (88) من أهل جنة عدن.

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report from ʿĀʾisha, from the Prophet, gives the phrase rawḥ wa-rayḥān.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه أنه قال: «فروح وريحان»

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads rawḥ with fatḥa; the other named readers and the rest read rūḥ, understood as rest in the grave, while rawḥ can mean life without death and rayḥān means provision.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الحسن كذلك، والأعمش وعاصم والسلمي وأهل المدينة وسائر القراء (فروح)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fasalām laka means a greeting confirming that the person is among the right-hand people; the omitted particle an is understood from the clause’s sense.
rows.anchor: أي: فذلك مسلم لك أنك من أصحاب اليمين، وألقيت أن وهو معناها كما تقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the greeting may be a prayer or blessing, like wishing a person prosperity; with nominative salām, it is a supplication.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون كالدعاء له، كقولك: فسقيا لك من الرجال، وإن رفعت السلام فهو دعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥad and shayʾ can substitute for each other when referring to people; shayʾ can refer to nonpeople, where aḥad cannot.
rows.anchor: وأحد يصلح في موضع- شيء، وشيء يصلح في موضع أحد في الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a believing wife leaves for Mecca as an unbeliever and there is no treaty, then the Muslims gain spoils, they should pay her former husband’s dower from the spoils before the fifth is taken.
rows.anchor: يقول: أعجزكم إن ذهبت امرأة فلحقت بأهل مكة كافرة، وليس بينكم وبينهم عهد فعاقبتم

rows.speaker: مسروق
rows.claim: Masrūq reads fa-ʿāqabtum and explains it as gaining spoils.
rows.anchor: عن مسروق أنه قرأ: «فعاقبتم» ، وفسرها: فغنمتم

rows.speaker: حميد الأعرج
rows.claim: Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj reads fa-ʿaqqabtum with a doubled consonant; Farrāʾ compares it to paired forms such as taṣʿaru and taṣāʿaru.
rows.anchor: وقرأها حميد الأعرج: فعقبتم مشددة ، وهي كقولك: تصعر، وتصاعر

rows.speaker: السلمى
rows.claim: Al-Sulamī alone is reported to read the prohibition against killing children in the form quoted here.
rows.anchor: قرأها السلمى وحده: ولا يقتلن أولادهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet sat at Ṣafā beside ʿUmar and women including Hind pledged not to associate partners with God, steal, or commit adultery; Hind asked whether a free woman would fornicate, and ʿUmar laughed.
rows.anchor: فجاءه النساء يبايعنه وفيهن هند بنت عتبة، فلما قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه: «لا يشركن بالله شيئا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on killing children addresses the pre-Islamic practice of burying daughters alive; Hind replied that the women had raised their children young while the Muslims killed them as adults.
rows.anchor: هذا فيما كان أهل الجاهلية يئدون، فبويعوا على ألا يفعلوا، فقالت هند: قد ربيناهم صغارا، وقتلتموهم كبارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The slander between a woman’s hands and feet is a claim that a child she picked up is her husband’s offspring.
rows.anchor: كانت المرأة تلتقط المولود، فتقول لزوجها: هذا ولدي منك. فذلك البهتان المفترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whom God is angry with despair of the afterlife’s reward and bliss, as disbelievers who have died and entered their graves have no worldly bliss left.
rows.anchor: يقول: من نعيم الآخرة وثوابها، كما يئس الكفار من أهل القبور، يقول: علموا ألا نعيم لهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the comparison as disbelievers despairing of the reward and bliss of the afterlife for those in the graves.
rows.anchor: ويقال: كما يئس الكفار من أصحاب القبور: من ثواب الآخرة ونعيمها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyukum is not directly governed by the test verb because an omitted verb of looking intervenes, as in testing to see which is most obedient; a verb like strike cannot omit that look.
rows.anchor: كما تقول في الكلام: بلوتكم لأنظر أيكم أطوع

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud is reported to read min tafūt, using the form without alif after the fāʾ.
rows.anchor: أن عبد الله بن مسعود قرأ. «من تفوت»

rows.speaker: علقمة
rows.claim: ʿAlqama is reported to read tafūt, as do Yaḥyā, Abdullah’s companions, the Medinans, and ʿĀṣim.
rows.anchor:
عن علقمة:
أنه قرأ: «تفوت» وهي قراءة يحيى ، وأصحاب عبد الله

rows.speaker: أهل البصرة
rows.claim: The Basrans read tafāwut; Farrāʾ says their form and tafūt are equivalent, like taṣʿar and taṣāʿar.
rows.anchor: وأهل البصرة يقرءون: «تفاوت» وهما بمنزلة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafāwut means difference or inconsistency in creation.
rows.anchor: التفاوت: الاختلاف، أي: هل ترى في خلقه من اختلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no earlier verb for farjiʿ to refer back to; mā tarā is effectively an instruction to look, followed by look again.
rows.anchor: فارجع البصر، وليس قبله فعل مذكور، فيكون الرجوع على ذلك الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fuṭūr means cracks and splits.
rows.anchor: وأما الفطور فالصدوع والشقوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāsiʾ means humbled or abased, and ḥasīr means weary and exhausted, like a camel worn down after being turned back.
rows.anchor: يريد: صاغرا، وهو حسير كليل، كما يحسر البعير والإبل إذا قومت عن هزال وكلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamayyazu min al-ghayẓ means the fire nearly tears itself apart in anger against them.
rows.anchor: تميز من الغيظ (8) تقطع عليهم غيظا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular dhنب is used because a sin is an act; a singular act attached to a group can stand for the sum of their deeds.
rows.anchor: لأن في الذنب فعلا، وكل واحد أضفته إلى قوم بعد أن يكون فعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caller was al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada, who challenged God to send stones if Muhammad’s message was true; he was captured at Badr and executed with ʿUqba.
rows.anchor: وهو: النضر [بن الحارث] بن كلدة، قال: اللهم إن كان ما يقول محمد هو الحق من عندك فأمطر علينا حجارة من السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment is for the disbelievers, and wāqiʿ is an adjective of punishment; the lām in lil-kāfirīn modifies punishment rather than the adjective.
rows.anchor: يريد: للكافرين، والواقع من نعت العذاب. واللام التي في الكافرين دخلت للعذاب لا للواقع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhī al-maʿārij describes God because angels ascend to Him.
rows.anchor: من صفة الله عز وجل لأن الملائكة تعرج إلى الله عز وجل، فوصف نفسه بذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ascent would take non-angels fifty thousand years, whereas angels ascend; this explains the duration assigned to the day.
rows.anchor: يقول: لو صعد غير الملائكة لصعدوا في قدر خمسين ألف سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers agree on feminine taʿruju; Abdullah is reported to read masculine yaʿruju, and Farrāʾ accepts either form.
rows.anchor: وأما (يعرج) ، فالقراء مجتمعون على التاء، وذكر بعض المشيخة عن زهير عن أبى إسحق الهمداني قال: قرأ عبد الله «يعرج» بالياء

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash says he heard no one recite yaʿruju, only taʿruju; Farrāʾ nevertheless accepts both forms.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعمش: ما سمعت أحدا يقرؤها إلا بالتاء. وكل صواب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They regard the resurrection as far off, while God calls it near because anything that is coming is near.
rows.anchor: يريد : البعث، ونراه نحن قريبا لأن كل ما هو آت: قريب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A close relative will not ask about another relative; they recognize one another for an hour, then recognition ends.
rows.anchor: لا يسأل ذو قرابة عن قرابته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read the clause passively, meaning no one asks a person where his close relative is; Farrāʾ dislikes it because it conflicts with the explanation and the readers agree on the active form.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ بعضهم: (ولا يسأل حميم حميما ) لا يقال لحميم : أين حميمك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faṣīla means a person’s closest forefathers, to whom he traces his lineage.
rows.anchor: هي أصغر آبائه الذي إليه ينتمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person imagines ransom will deliver him from God’s punishment, but the following kallā rejects that hope.
rows.anchor: أي: ينجيه الافتداء من عذاب الله. قال الله عز وجل: «كلا» أي: لا ينجيه ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laẓā is a proper name for Hell, which is why it is indeclinable.
rows.anchor: ولظى: اسم من أسماء جهنم فلذلك لم يجره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazzāʿatan can be nominative as a second predicate after inna-hā laẓā, or laẓā and nazzāʿa can be predicated reciprocally with the pronoun as a support particle.
rows.anchor: مرفوع على قولك: إنها لظى، إنها نزاعة للشوى، وإن شئت جعلت الهاء عمادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-shawā are the hands, feet, and scalp skin; the scalp itself is called shawāt, and nonfatal parts are called shawā.
rows.anchor: والشوى: اليدان، والرجلان، وجلدة الرأس يقال لها: شواة، وما كان غير مقتل فهو شوى.
